title: Want a US Visa Interview in 10 Days? That Will Be $750 Extra.
excerpt: The State Department is launching a premium fast-track service for B1/B2 visa applicants starting July 1, just in time for the FIFA World Cup. For Indians facing 16-month wait times, it is both a lifeline and a tax on urgency.
body:
If you have ever applied for a US tourist or business visa from India, you know the drill: fill the DS-160, pay the $185 fee, and then wait. In some cities, that wait stretches to 16 months for an interview appointment. Abu Dhabi applicants face similar timelines. Istanbul, by contrast, gets you in within two weeks.

Starting July 1, the US State Department will offer a way to skip the line — for a price. A new pilot programme will let B1/B2 visa applicants pay an additional $750, on top of the standard $185 fee, to secure an interview appointment within 10 business days.

The catch: paying does not guarantee a visa. It only guarantees a faster interview slot. Every applicant still goes through the same biometric checks, background screening, and consular adjudication. And the $750 is non-refundable, whether the visa is approved or not.

## Built for the World Cup, but the Implications Are Permanent

The timing is no coincidence. The FIFA 2026 World Cup kicks off in the United States later this month, with more than a million foreign tourists expected to descend on American stadiums. The State Department explicitly cited the World Cup and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics as motivations for the pilot.

"In the wake of the 2026 FIFA World Cup and ahead of the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games in Los Angeles, the Department has determined that now is the time to test the demand for and provision of a new fee-based expedited interview appointment service," the notice published in the Federal Register states.

The pilot runs through December 31 at select embassies and consulates, which will be announced before the July 1 start date. The State Department estimates roughly 25,700 applicants per year will use the service, generating approximately $19.3 million in annual revenue.

## The Visa Bottleneck Is Largely Self-Made

The irony is not lost on immigration attorneys. The very backlogs this programme aims to relieve were created, in large part, by the Trump administration's own policies.

Over the past year, the administration has layered on new requirements that have slowed visa processing worldwide: $15,000 bonds for applicants from 50 countries (predominantly in Africa), mandatory disclosure of years of personal history including social media accounts, and — until a federal judge struck it down two days ago — a $100,000 fee on H-1B visa applications.

New York-based immigration attorney Michael Cataliotti told USA Today that the $750 fee is "an exorbitant amount in many of the countries where people are applying for these visas." For an Indian family trying to visit relatives in the US, $935 in total fees — with no guarantee of approval — is not a minor expense.

## What Indian Applicants Need to Know

The premium service applies only to B1 (business) and B2 (tourism/medical) non-immigrant visas. These are the visas most commonly used by Indian families visiting relatives, attending events, or seeking medical treatment in the United States. They typically allow stays of up to 180 days and are valid for 10 years.

Key details from the Federal Register filing:

- **Fee**: $750 on top of the standard $185 application fee
- **Guarantee**: An interview appointment within 10 business days of payment
- **No visa guarantee**: The expedited interview does not affect the outcome of the visa adjudication
- **Non-refundable**: The fee is not returned if the visa is denied
- **Availability**: Limited to select embassies and consulates (to be announced before July 1)
- **Duration**: July 1 through December 31, 2026, with possible extension

The programme will not affect processing times after the interview. Administrative processing — which can add weeks or months for applicants flagged for additional review — remains unchanged.

## A Two-Tier System Takes Shape

The $750 fast-track joins a growing suite of paid advantages in the US immigration system under the current administration. The "Trump Gold Card" offers permanent residence and a pathway to citizenship for $1 million. Visa bonds of up to $15,000 are required from applicants in certain countries to guarantee they will not overstay. And now, interview scheduling itself has become a premium product.

For the Indian diaspora, this is personal. India is one of the largest sources of B1/B2 visa applicants. Millions of NRIs have parents, siblings, and extended family who navigate this system every year — for weddings, medical emergencies, graduations, and the ordinary desire to visit family abroad.

The question the State Department's pilot raises is not whether there is demand for faster service. There obviously is. The question is whether a system that creates bottlenecks and then charges to bypass them is serving anyone fairly.

The embassies and consulates participating in the programme will be announced on the State Department's website before July 1. For Indians planning travel to the US this summer, the math just got more complicated.
